_about: Money Made Simple for Schools: 4 sample weekly mini-lessons (Jan 11 to Feb 1 2027 class dates), delivered to the school 2 weeks early. 'standard' names the 2021 National Standards for Personal Financial Education area each lesson supports. Read by ../build.py.

issues.source: MMS evergreen: 'Read your pay stub', 1099 Money Short #03 (where your paycheck goes)
issues.topic: Your first paycheck: where did the money go?
issues.subject: Lesson: why your paycheck is smaller than you expected
issues.preheader: Gross pay, net pay, and the three things taken out of almost every paycheck.
issues.headline: Where did my paycheck go?
issues.example: Jordan works 20 hours at $15 an hour. Gross pay: $300. Social Security: $18.60. Medicare: $4.35. Federal income tax withheld: $9.00. State tax: $6.00. Net pay (what lands in the bank): $261.95.
explain: **Gross pay** is what you earned before anything is taken out. **Net pay** is what you actually take home. The difference surprises almost everyone the first time.

Almost every paycheck has **Social Security (6.2%)** and **Medicare (1.45%)** taken out. These pay for benefits you can collect later. **Income tax** is also withheld, based on the W-4 form you fill in when you're hired. Many states take state income tax too.
issues.tell: Plan your spending around net pay, not gross pay. The number on the job ad isn't the number in your bank.
steps: **Work out Jordan's take-home pay** as a class: $300 minus each line in the example. Check that you get $261.95.
**Now your turn:** if you earned $12 an hour for 15 hours, what would Social Security and Medicare be? (Answer in the teacher notes.)
**Find the W-4** on IRS.gov and look at Step 1. That's the form you'll fill in at your first job.
quick_hits: Why do you think Social Security and Medicare are taken out of every paycheck, even for teenagers?
If your take-home pay is about 87% of your gross pay, how much would you actually have from a $500 paycheck?
issues.job: Name two things taken out of a paycheck, and say what each one pays for.

lobby.headline: Gross pay isn't what you take home.
bullets: Income tax: set by your W-4.

social.caption: This week's money lesson: why is your paycheck smaller than you expected? Gross pay is what you earned. Net pay is what you take home after Social Security (6.2%), Medicare (1.45%) and income tax come out. Plan your spending around net pay.
social.alt: Money lesson: gross pay isn't what you take home. Social Security 6.2%. Medicare 1.45%. Income tax set by your W-4.

brief.Standard: Earning Income (2021 National Standards for Personal Financial Education, grade 12 benchmarks on taxes and payroll deductions).
brief.Timing: 2 min slide, 6 min activity, 2 min exit ticket.
brief.Answer key: $12 × 15 = $180 gross. Social Security: $180 × 6.2% = $11.16. Medicare: $180 × 1.45% = $2.61. Income tax depends on the W-4 and other income, so the example uses made-up amounts.
brief.Watch for: Students asking what to put on their own W-4. Point them to the IRS instructions and a parent or guardian; don't advise on individual forms.

issues.source: MMS evergreen: 'Needs, wants and the 50/30/20 start', carousel #05
issues.topic: Needs, wants and a simple budget
issues.subject: Lesson: a budget that takes 10 minutes
issues.preheader: Sort needs from wants, then try one common starting split: 50/30/20.
issues.headline: Needs, wants and a 10-minute budget
issues.example: Maya takes home $800 a month from a part-time job. Using 50/30/20 as a starting point: $400 for needs (phone, gas, her share of groceries), $240 for wants (food out, games, concerts), $160 for savings.
explain: A **need** is something you must pay for to live, work or go to school: housing, food, transportation, a phone you need for work. A **want** is nice to have. Some things are both: you need shoes, you want the $180 ones.

One common starting point is **50/30/20**: about half of take-home pay for needs, 30% for wants, 20% for savings. It's a rule of thumb, not a law. When rent is high, needs take more, and that's normal.
issues.tell: A budget is a plan for your money before you spend it, not a list of what you already spent.
steps: **Sort this list into needs and wants** with a partner: bus pass, streaming service, school lunch, new phone case, car insurance, concert ticket. Some might be both: say why.
**Use Maya's example** to work out 50/30/20 for $600 a month.
**Pick one savings goal** you'd want 20% to go toward, and how many months it would take.
quick_hits: Is a phone a need or a want? Does it depend on the person?
What would you cut first if your income dropped by $100 a month?
issues.job: Write one need, one want and one thing that could be either, and explain the last one.

lobby.headline: Plan your money before you spend it.

social.caption: This week's money lesson: needs, wants and a 10-minute budget. Try 50/30/20 as a starting point: about half of take-home pay for needs, 30% for wants and 20% for savings. It's a rule of thumb, so adjust it to your life.
social.alt: Money lesson: plan your money before you spend it. Needs first, then wants. Try 50/30/20 as a start. Save something.

brief.Standard: Spending and Saving (2021 National Standards, budgeting and saving goals).
brief.Timing: 2 min slide, 6 min sort and math, 2 min exit ticket.
brief.Watch for: Students whose families are under financial stress. Keep examples about made-up people, and don't ask students to share their own family's income or bills.

issues.source: MMS evergreen: 'What actually moves your credit score', carousel #14
issues.subject: Lesson: what goes into a credit score
issues.preheader: The five parts of a FICO score, and why paying on time matters most.
issues.headline: What's in a credit score?
issues.example: Sam gets a first credit card with a $500 limit, puts a $40 phone bill on it each month, and pays it in full on the due date with autopay. A year later Sam has a short but perfect payment record.
explain: A **credit score** is a number lenders use to guess how likely you are to pay back a loan. It can affect renting an apartment, a car loan, and sometimes the cost of insurance.

The most widely used score, FICO, says it's made from five ingredients: **payment history (35%)**, **amounts owed (30%)**, **length of credit history (15%)**, **new credit (10%)** and **credit mix (10%)**.
issues.tell: Paying on time, every time, is the biggest part of your score. Autopay for at least the minimum is the easiest way to protect it.
steps: **Rank the five ingredients** from biggest to smallest without looking, then check.
**Read Sam's example** and say which ingredients Sam is building, and how.
**Find the official free credit report site** (AnnualCreditReport.com). Why might someone your age check it?
quick_hits: Why would a landlord care about your credit score?
What's one risk of having a credit card, and one way to avoid it?
issues.job: Name the biggest ingredient in a FICO score and one habit that builds it.

lobby.headline: Pay on time. It's 35% of your score.

social.caption: This week's money lesson: what's in a credit score? Payment history is 35% of a FICO score, the biggest part, followed by amounts owed (30%), length of history, new credit and credit mix. Paying on time is the habit that matters most. Free credit reports: AnnualCreditReport.com.
social.alt: Money lesson: pay on time, it's 35% of your score. Payment history 35%. Amounts owed 30%. Free reports at AnnualCreditReport.com.

brief.Standard: Managing Credit (2021 National Standards, credit reports and scores).
brief.Timing: 2 min slide, 6 min ranking and example, 2 min exit ticket.
brief.Answer key: Payment history 35%, amounts owed 30%, length of history 15%, new credit 10%, credit mix 10%. Sam builds payment history and a low amount owed, and starts length of history.
brief.Watch for: Don't recommend specific cards or banks. Credit card rules for people under 21 are strict; students should ask a parent or guardian before applying.

issues.source: Scam Decoded: fake job offers and the overpayment check
issues.topic: Fake job offers and the overpayment trick
issues.subject: Lesson: the job offer that sends you a check
issues.preheader: A 'job' that pays you first and asks for money back is a scam. Here's how it works.
issues.headline: The job that pays you first
issues.example: A text: "Hi! Remote assistant job, $25/hr, no interview. We'll mail you a $1,200 check. Keep $300 for your first week, buy $900 in gift cards for office supplies and send us the codes."
explain: Fake job offers target students because you're looking for flexible work. The "employer" sends a check, asks you to deposit it and send part of the money somewhere else: gift cards, a payment app, crypto.
The check bounces days later, sometimes after the bank has made the money available. You owe the bank the whole amount, and the money you sent is gone.
issues.tell: A real job never pays you before you start and then asks you to send money back.
steps: **Spot the red flags** in the example as a class. (Hint: there are at least four.)
**Look up how real jobs hire:** an application, an interview, tax forms like the W-4. Compare that to the text.
**Write a reply** you could send, or decide not to reply at all and say why.
quick_hits: Why do scammers like gift cards and payment apps?
Who could you ask if you weren't sure a job offer was real?
issues.job: List two red flags of a fake job offer.

lobby.headline: A job that pays you first is a scam.

social.caption: This week's money lesson: fake job offers. If a "job" sends you a check and asks you to send part of it back by gift card, payment app or crypto, it's a scam. The check bounces and you owe the bank. Real jobs don't pay you before you start.
social.alt: Money lesson: a job that pays you first is a scam. No interview is a red flag. Never send money back. Gift cards mean scam.

brief.Standard: Managing Risk (2021 National Standards, fraud and identity protection).
brief.Timing: 2 min slide, 6 min red flags and reply, 2 min exit ticket.
brief.Answer key: Red flags: unsolicited text, no interview, pay before work, a check for more than owed, gift cards, send codes.
brief.Watch for: A student who may already have deposited a check like this. Tell them privately to talk to a parent or guardian and their bank right away, and report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

sources.name: FTC: How to spot, avoid, and report fake check scams
